documents: Published paper: Smets, Weemstra & Evers (2022), JGR Oceans 127, e2022JC018451 (PDF, 26 pp.)
pages_convention: printed journal pages (n of 26), which equal PDF pages counted from 1

entry.evidence: we introduce a specific workflow to exploit repetitive hydroacoustic underwater source activity

steps.action: Frame the problem: passive SOFAR thermometry from Green's functions between IMS hydrophones is hampered by single-sided, non-isotropic wavefields and bathymetric blocking.
steps.quote: An accurate estimation of a Green's function and the phase velocity between two IMS hydrophones is therefore challenging.

steps.action: Take up the travel-time method of Wu et al. (2020) and the RMS-envelope hydrophone-seismometer cross-correlation of Metz et al. (2016) as starting methods.
steps.quote: [...] et al. (2020) introduced a method to infer basin-scale deep-ocean temperature changes from sound waves generated by repeating ridge earthquakes.

steps.action: Propose a two-location method pairing a hydrophone triplet with a three-component seismometer that keeps phase and spectral information, uses vertical and radial components, and is released as open code.
steps.quote: We extend the two-receiver method of Metz et al. (2016) to a two-location method composed of a triplet hydrophone station and a three-component broadband seismometer

steps.action: Select H03S and IU.RAR.10 from the candidate triplets and seismometers on line of sight, noise, obstruction, instrument response and data availability, discarding H03N, H10S, RAR.00 and the other island stations.
steps.quote: we only consider the three-component Streckeisen seismometer at Rarotonga with SEED-IDs IU.RAR.10.BH[1,2,Z]

steps.action: Compute the slowness and back-azimuth errors caused by the 0.6° tilt of H03S to justify planar, horizontal-plane array processing.
steps.quote: For near-horizontal signals, the errors are minor.

steps.action: Build the processing chain: ObsPy preprocessing to 50 sps with response removal and rotation, then an unbiased, normalized frequency-domain cross-correlation over 24 hr windows at 3 hr increments.
steps.quote: Hence, a sample rate of 50 sps facilitates the cross-correlation of hydroacoustic and T-phase observations.

steps.action: Show an example CCF (15 January 2015) whose peak lag gives a SOFAR channel sound speed, with a modal spectrogram signature.
steps.quote: Time lag and indicated velocity at the peak CCF corresponds to the SOFAR channel speed of sound.

steps.action: Compare the spectrogram's modal arrival order with the dispersion expected for SOFAR propagation (Munk 2006).
steps.quote: with the expected SOFAR channel dispersion: high-frequency modes are more narrowly confined to the SOFAR channel axis

steps.action: Observe near-identical CCF signatures for the three hydrophones with both vertical and radial components, then compute CCFs for six receiver couples, 2014-2020.
steps.quote: The CCFs with each of the three hydroacoustic sensors exhibit a very similar signature, with near-identical velocities at the peak correlation.

steps.action: Define a source-activity selection criterion: CCF signal-to-noise ratio above 10 in all six couples (coincidence trigger) for at least one day.
steps.quote: is defined as a period for which the S/N of six CCFs exceed the prescribed threshold of 10

steps.action: Describe the detected MVC activity periods per year and per month, which are uniform across years but not within the year.
steps.quote: The activity distribution over the years is relatively uniform; the activity distribution during the year is not.

steps.action: Reject the peak-envelope time lag as a travel-time estimator because it jumps between cycles and modal peaks (Figure 6).
steps.quote: Hence, utilizing the peak amplitude time lag will make acoustic thermometry erratic.

steps.action: Estimate horizontal slowness, back azimuth and apparent velocity by least-squares plane-wave fitting of inter-element CCF delays.
steps.quote: The slowness vectors associated with MVC activity cluster around the slowness values one would expect for a signal originating at the MVC.

steps.action: Repeat the plane-wave estimation with the radial seismic component (supplement Figures S1-S2) and find comparable results.
steps.quote: Results for the radial seismic component are comparable

steps.action: Check the bearing offset against the known -1.3° back-azimuth bias of H03S from airgun shots (Metz et al. 2018), and show that activity filtering removes other events (Figure 7).
steps.quote: [...] the estimated plane wave bearing and the actual bearing (see Table 2) closely approximates the expected back azimuth error

steps.action: Add plane-wave limits (241-243°, 1,490-1,495 m/s) as a second selection criterion, then design the time-lapse analysis: 2D normalized cross-correlation of CCF spectrograms in 3-6 and 6-12 Hz octaves with trimean filtering of spurious time steps, in place of phase tracking.
steps.quote: Therefore, this study applies time-lapse analysis to the spectrograms (S) of the eligible CCFs signal windows

steps.action: Adopt the expectation that travel time changes chiefly reflect path-averaged temperature, with salinity and current effects negligible (Munk 2006; Dushaw et al. 2009).
steps.quote: The travel time changes primarily depend on changes in the deep-ocean temperature (Munk, 2006).

steps.action: Compute trimmed weighted mean lag-time variations with 95% confidence, fit WLS linear trends with 20,000 bootstrap estimates, and find Lomb-Scargle periodicities of about 1.9 yr (3-6 Hz) and 1.1 yr (6-12 Hz).
steps.quote: The travel time change over time reveals a complex periodic variation as well as a robust linear trend.

steps.action: Compare the trends across the four receiver pairs (including the radial component) and the triplet average (Table 3): about -22 to -34 ms/yr at 3-6 Hz and about -50 to -55 ms/yr at 6-12 Hz.
steps.quote: Linear Regression of the Trimmed Weighted Mean Lag Time Variation

steps.action: State the vertical-plane (ZR) phase lags expected for body waves (near zero), Rayleigh waves (about 90°) and Love waves.
steps.quote: Hence, body waves correspond to a near-zero phase lag between the CCFs.

steps.action: Compare the observed ZR phase-lag spectral density of H03S1-RAR with those expectations and find frequency-dependent mixed wave types.
steps.quote: The phase lag response indicates a mixture of dilatational body waves, at 2 and 4 Hz

steps.action: Keep the claim that the workflow retrieves hydroacoustic travel time variations usable as a proxy for path-averaged deep-ocean temperature change.
steps.quote: This study demonstrates the retrieval of hydroacoustic travel time variations by time-lapse analysis of a triplet hydrophone station relative to a three-component broadband seismometer.

steps.action: Attribute the decreasing trend to net warming and name ocean-circulation oscillations (wind, tides, ENSO, Antarctic Circumpolar Current) as possible alternative or contributing causes, without testing them.
steps.quote: The decreasing trend may correspond to lower values of ocean circulation oscillations, almost entirely controlled by surface wind forcing and deep water tides

steps.action: Compare the larger trend in the high-frequency band with the expectation of strongest warming near the surface, given that high-frequency modes stay near the SOFAR axis.
steps.quote: The difference in trend between the octave bands agrees with the difference in the vertical sampling of the SOFAR channel.

tree.answer: Repeated Monowai hydroacoustic signals at H03S and RAR, whose travel time varies over time
No; travel time variations are inferred from time-lapse spectrogram correlation, and temperature only by proxy
A reusable workflow (cookbook) to extract deep-ocean travel time variations
No rivals tested; peak-lag estimator excluded as a method; circulation oscillations named after the fact
No distinct predictions derived for rival causes of the trend
Conditions found: a natural repeating volcanic source recorded by archival IMS and IRIS stations

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Yes; repeated MVC activity episodes 2014-2020 supply about 2,100 eligible time steps
Partly; consistent across receiver pairs, the radial component and the known array bias, but no independent data or method
Kept: workflow characterized and trends estimated with CI; warming attribution assumed
Not documented; no review file (two anonymous reviewers thanked)

end.claim: A two-location workflow (hydrophone triplet against a three-component seismometer, with activity and slowness selection and spectrogram time-lapse) retrieves frequency-dependent travel time variations from Monowai signals; these show a periodic pattern on a decreasing linear trend attributed to warming.

decisive_move.sentence: The time-lapse 2D cross-correlation of band-limited CCF spectrograms, applied after activity and plane-wave selection, is what yields the travel time variations; without it the peak-lag estimate was erratic.

gates.evidence: Archival IMS and IRIS data, not acquired under a hypothesis. The selection was checked against the known MVC bearing and the −1.3° array bias, and trends agree across receiver pairs, but the warming attribution is assumed rather than tested against independent temperature data. The S/N threshold of 10 and the weights (μΔf = 0, σΔf = 0.1 Hz) are stated without any pre-registration.

imports.field: nuclear test-ban verification (CTBTO International Monitoring System)

imports.item: Unbiased digital cross-correlation after Bendat & Piersol (1987)
Generalized two-dimensional correlation applied to spectrograms
Trimean, weighted summary measures, bootstrap and Student's t confidence intervals
Scikit-learn weighted least squares with bootstrap
Lomb-Scargle periodogram for unevenly sampled series

novelty_claims.quote: In particular, we introduce a specific workflow to exploit repetitive hydroacoustic underwater source activity
We extend the two-receiver method of Metz et al. (2016) to a two-location method

limits: Only the published paper was supplied, so no review sequence could be coded. The paper makes no explicit 'first' claim; the novelty claims listed are statements of new methods. The temperature attribution rests on cited theory (Munk 2006; Dushaw et al. 2009): no inversion for temperature is done and no comparison is made with independent ocean data (Argo, ECCO, WOA). The warming attribution is therefore at most best_explanation, and the ocean-circulation alternative is named but not tested. The trend estimates (Table 3) stand as estimate_with_resolution, with non-uniform seasonal sampling acknowledged. The ZR phase-lag wave-type reading is a qualitative interpretation. The checks across receiver pairs share one seismometer and one triplet, so they are not independent replications (inference). Weighting parameters, the S/N threshold, the trimean cut-off and the STFT window are single choices with no reported sensitivity test. No independent data or second method is applied to the travel times, so triangulation is absent. Only one source-station pair is processed.

disagreements.target: Metz et al. (2016) normalized RMS-amplitude cross-correlation
disagreements.support: The authors argue that band-passing and RMS envelopes discard spectral and phase information, and their workflow retains both.
disagreements.quote: Notwithstanding retrieving the relative travel time, many spectral and all phase [...] .

disagreements.target: Metz et al. (2016) use of IU.RAR.00.BHZ (Geotech KS-54000) as reference
disagreements.support: The instrument response and data availability of RAR.00 are described as inferior, and the Streckeisen at location 10 is used instead.
disagreements.quote: The seismometer has a non-flat passband and a complete 180° phase shift between 1 Hz and the Nyquist.

disagreements.target: Green's-function passive thermometry between IMS stations (Evers et al., 2017; Woolfe et al., 2015)
disagreements.support: Single-sided Fresnel zones, a non-isotropic field, few unblocked station couples and small triplet aperture make Green's-function phase-velocity estimation unreliable.
disagreements.quote: An accurate estimation of a Green's function and the phase velocity between two IMS hydrophones is therefore challenging.

disagreements.target: W. Wu et al. (2020) seismic ocean thermometry using P-wave constraints
disagreements.support: Direct cross-correlation with a near-source T-phase station gives the relative travel time without needing a seismic phase reference.
disagreements.quote: In contrast to W. Wu et al. (2020), the cross-correlation directly yields the relative travel time not needing a specific seismic phase

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Green's-function retrieval by interferometry between IMS hydrophones
alternatives_considered.reason: Single-sided, non-isotropic wavefield, bathymetric blocking and small triplet aperture

alternatives_considered.chosen: Retain phase and spectral information with minimal preprocessing
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Normalized RMS-amplitude cross-correlation in one-minute windows (Metz et al., 2016)
alternatives_considered.reason: RMS approach loses spectral and all phase information

alternatives_considered.chosen: Vertical and radial seismic components only
alternatives_considered.reason: none given at the point of choice; later, Love waves are not expected to couple into the water column
H03N partly obstructed by a seamount (lower S/N); H10S electronic noise; analysis limited to one station to limit divergence

alternatives_considered.alternatives: IU.RAR.00 KS-54000 borehole (20 sps); 100 sps HHZ channel
alternatives_considered.reason: Non-flat passband and phase shift of RAR.00 with data only 2010-2018; HHZ availability too short

alternatives_considered.alternatives: NIUE, AFI, RAO, NFK; Fiji stations
alternatives_considered.reason: Only RAR shows a pronounced MVC signal; NIUE high-pass filtered, others blocked, Fiji data not public

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Increment equal to the time lag of interest (rule of thumb)
alternatives_considered.reason: Long window suppresses noise and events; 3 hr increment limits computational effort

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Time lag of peak (envelope) CCF amplitude
alternatives_considered.reason: Peak time lag is not robust (cycle skipping, modal jumps)

alternatives_considered.chosen: 2D cross-correlation of spectrograms in two octave bands
alternatives_considered.alternatives: 1D cross-correlation of CCF signal windows; narrow-band filtering with phase tracking
alternatives_considered.reason: 1D correlation does not quantify source-signature change; sporadic activity causes cycle skipping that makes phase tracking impossible

alternatives_considered.chosen: Travel time variations as a temperature proxy without inversion
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Travel-time inversion for temperature (Wu et al., 2020); full waveform inversion
alternatives_considered.reason: Inversion not carried out in this study; FWI more applicable if the modal structure changes

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Multi-time-window FFT, wavelet scaleogram, Fisher analysis with phase-aligned cross-spectrum
alternatives_considered.reason: none given (recommended for future work because of the time-frequency trade-off and loss of phase)
